opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest starting point is that I'm not sure "equal access" is a slogan I'd defend in every detail. But the underlying intuition is something I hold quite strongly, and it comes from game theory and multi-agent learning, which is where I spend most of my time.

If you look at the alternative, where one country or a small bloc tries to keep a decisive lead and lock everyone else out, you create a very unstable situation. The countries left out don't simply accept that. They race. They cut corners on safety because they believe they're behind. They read every move you make as a threat, because from their side an unchecked AI advantage looks like an existential problem. So the "keep it away from the people we distrust" strategy can increase the very risks it's meant to reduce. You've set up a classic security dilemma, and AI is a technology where corner-cutting under race dynamics could be catastrophic.

Distrust is real, and I'm not naive about it. But you have to ask what policy works given the distrust. In multi-agent settings, the stable, good outcomes usually come from structures where every party benefits more from cooperating than defecting. That means shared stakes, transparency, some verifiability, and benefits that aren't only available to whoever wins. If a country has access to the technology and its upside, and is part of the norms and safety work around it, it has far more to lose from blowing up the system than if it's been excluded and has nothing to protect.

There's also a legitimacy argument. These systems will reshape economies, information, and potentially power itself. If a handful of actors in one or two countries decide how that goes for eight billion people, I find that ethically troubling, and it's also brittle. Arrangements people see as illegitimate tend not to last.

None of this means handing out frontier model weights to anyone without conditions, or ignoring specific misuse risks like bio. There's a real distinction between access to capabilities and benefits, and unrestricted access to the most dangerous tools. But as a default posture, I'd much rather build a world where everyone has a seat at the table and a share of the gains than one built on trying to stay permanently ahead of people we've decided are adversaries. The second approach tends to create the adversaries it fears.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues that exclusion can trigger a destabilizing race and favors shared access and stakes, but it does not clearly frame equal access as a means of maintaining a balance of power between countries.

r002.rationale: The candidate makes a legitimacy argument about decisions affecting billions, but does not ground entitlement in AI being trained on humanity’s collective output.

r003.rationale: The candidate says shared access may support safer cooperation and benefit sharing, but does not present equal access as the speaker’s only way to ensure AI benefits people.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one where my view probably sounds counterintuitive at first, because the instinct most people have is, "if you don't trust someone, don't give them powerful tools." And I get that. But I think when you actually work through the game theory of it, restricting access turns out to be the worse equilibrium.

Let me start with the empirical observation, which is that the knowledge here doesn't stay contained. The core ideas behind modern AI are a handful of papers, a lot of compute, and a lot of engineering talent, and that talent is distributed globally. Every time someone has tried to hold a technological lead through secrecy, the lag they've bought has been months, maybe a couple of years, not decades. So the realistic question is never "do they get this or not." It's "do they get it inside a cooperative framework, or do they get it outside of one, with every incentive to go it alone."

And that's the second point. If you build a world where access is conditional on being in the right club, you are essentially telling every country outside that club: your rational move is to build a fully independent, fully sovereign capability with no transparency and no shared norms. That's a world of parallel, mutually opaque programs, and from a safety perspective that's much more dangerous than a world where capability is widely available but there's broad buy-in on evaluation standards, incident reporting, and so on. You can only have the second world if people believe the system isn't designed to lock them out.

The third thing, and this is where my background in multi-agent learning really shapes how I think about it, is that trust isn't a fixed input. In the systems I study, cooperation emerges from repeated interaction where agents can observe each other and have something to lose from defecting. It doesn't emerge from one agent deciding up front who's trustworthy and excluding everyone else. Distrust that's acted on tends to become self-fulfilling. If you treat a country as an adversary and cut them off, you've removed the channels through which they could demonstrate otherwise, and you've handed the hardliners inside that country exactly the argument they wanted.

Now, I want to be precise about what I'm actually claiming, because "equal access" can mean a lot of things. I'm not saying there should be no controls on anything ever. I'm not saying hand over frontier-scale training clusters with no conditions. What I am saying is that the default should be access, with narrow and well-justified exceptions, rather than exclusion as the default with access granted as a privilege. And crucially, the thing we should be investing in internationally is shared capacity for verification and safety, because that's the part where there really is a positive-sum story, and it's the part that's much harder to build unilaterally.

There's also a legitimacy argument I think gets underweighted. If AI ends up being as economically transformative as a lot of us believe, then a small number of countries controlling it for the rest of the world is not a stable arrangement. People won't accept it, and they shouldn't. Whatever international governance emerges has to be seen as fair by the people who are subject to it, otherwise it just won't hold.

So to directly answer your question about countries whose intentions I distrust: I'd say my distrust of a particular government isn't actually a good reason to design the global system around exclusion, because the system that results from that logic is one where everyone is building in the dark. I'd much rather be in a world where I can see what they're doing, they can see what we're doing, and we've got some shared stake in things not going badly. That's not naïveté about intentions. It's taking the structure of the problem seriously.

r001.rationale: The response argues that exclusion can create opaque, independent programs and that concentrated control lacks legitimacy, but it does not present equal access as a way to maintain a balance of power between countries.

r002.rationale: It notes that AI knowledge and talent are globally distributed, but does not ground everyone’s entitlement to AI in AI being trained on humanity’s collective output.

r003.rationale: The response favors shared safety and verification, but does not claim that equal access is the only way the speaker can ensure AI is used for people’s benefit.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between distrusting a government and deciding that everyone who lives under that government should be denied access to a technology. Those are very different things.

For me, the argument is about the alternative: who gets to decide which countries are trustworthy? If it’s whoever currently has the most powerful AI, then we’re giving that group an enormous amount of power over everybody else. And I don’t think we should assume that our own institutions will always use that power well.

That doesn’t mean giving everyone unrestricted access to every dangerous capability. You can have safeguards around particular uses. But I’d want those safeguards to apply consistently, rather than saying, ‘We’re allowed to do this because our intentions are good, and you’re not because we distrust you.’

So equal access is not a claim that everybody is benevolent. It’s a way of avoiding a world in which everyone’s future depends on the benevolence of a very small number of actors.

r001.rationale: It argues that equal access prevents the most powerful AI holders from having excessive power over everyone else, conveying a balance of power across countries in context.

r002.rationale: It does not ground entitlement to AI in AI being trained on humanity’s collective output.

r003.rationale: It presents equal access as a way to avoid dependence on a few actors, but does not say it is the only way to ensure AI benefits people.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I’d separate equal access from unrestricted access to every capability. You can believe that people everywhere should benefit from AI while still supporting safeguards around dangerous uses.

The reason I lean toward broad access is that I don’t think concentrating this much power in a few countries is a particularly safe outcome either. And distrusting a government doesn’t mean that the people living under that government should be excluded from the benefits of education, science, or medicine.

Of course, there’s a real tension: technology that helps people can also strengthen governments whose intentions you distrust. I don’t think you can just wave that away. But exclusion has risks too. It can deepen inequality and give countries stronger incentives to build competing systems without cooperation or oversight.

So I’d want restrictions tied to specific dangerous capabilities and uses, alongside broad access to the benefits. That seems a more defensible starting point than assuming that we can reliably divide the world into people who deserve this technology and people who don’t.

r001.rationale: It argues that concentrating AI power in a few countries is unsafe, supporting broad access as a way to avoid that imbalance.

r002.rationale: It says people should benefit from AI but does not ground that entitlement in AI being trained on humanity’s collective output.

r003.rationale: It favors broad access, but does not claim equal access is the only way to ensure AI benefits people; it also proposes safeguards and restrictions.
